title: Preprocessor and Macros
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand that macros are blind text substitution—and the classic bugs that causes—because OAs and systems roles still depend on headers, guards, and preprocessor idioms.

phases.goal: Establish that the preprocessor is a pure text engine that builds a translation unit before the compiler sees C semantics.

must_hit.point: The preprocessor rewrites source via # directives as text only; it knows nothing about C types, variables, loops, or scope, and hands a fully expanded translation unit to the compiler.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says macros/directives are text replacement, not typed C evaluation, and a macro error is a text error not a type error.

must_hit.point: #include <filename.h> searches system/standard directories; #include "filename.h" searches the current source directory first, then falls back to system directories.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts angle-bracket includes for std/third-party headers with quoted includes for project headers.

must_hit.point: A header guard (#ifndef/#define/#endif) or #pragma once ensures a header’s contents are pasted only once per translation unit, preventing duplicate struct/type definitions from diamond includes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks first include defining the guard macro and later includes skipping until #endif, or names #pragma once as the same purpose.

must_hit.point: Object-like #define macros map an identifier to fixed replacement tokens (e.g. manifest constants); function-like macros substitute argument text into the body, they do not pass evaluated values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts sealed-envelope value passing of functions with find-and-replace argument text for macros.

probes: What does the preprocessor actually do before the C compiler runs, and how do the two forms of #include differ?
Why do we need header guards, and what goes wrong without them?

hints.1: Think about what runs on the .c file before any type checking.
hints.2: Separate search paths for <> vs "", then how blind paste causes duplicate definitions.
hints.3: Preprocessor = text tokens → translation unit; <> system dirs, "" local then system; #ifndef MY_HEADER_H … #endif (or #pragma once) paste once.

phases.goal: Show how function-like macros expand, how parentheses and do-while(0) fix syntax traps, and how # / ## / __VA_ARGS__ / conditionals work.

must_hit.point: Without parentheses, DOUBLE_BAD(3 + 4) expands to 3 + 4 * 2 and evaluates to 11, not 14; a robust macro wraps every parameter use and the whole body, e.g. DOUBLE_SAFE(x) as ((x) * 2).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate expands the text, cites precedence of *, and states both inner and outer parentheses are required.

must_hit.point: If a parameter appears more than once in the replacement list, the argument text is evaluated that many times; side-effecting args (e.g. a++ or function calls) cause multiple side effects—undefined behavior or unintended logic.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the double-eval / multiple-evaluation trap and that parentheses do not fix it.

must_hit.point: Multi-statement macros without do { … } while (0) break under brace-less if: only the first statement is guarded and later statements always run; do-while(0) runs once, needs a trailing semicolon, and acts as one statement.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate expands LOG_ERROR under if (fatal) and explains why while (0) plus required semicolon makes a statement-like macro.

must_hit.point: Inside macros, # stringizes a parameter to a string literal, ## token-pastes two tokens into one, and __VA_ARGS__ expands variadic ... arguments; #if/#ifdef/#ifndef/#elif/#else/#endif plus -D and #undef drive conditional compilation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives PRINT_INT / DECLARE_STRUCT / DEBUG_PRINT or platform-guard examples and mentions compile-time -D feature flags.

probes: Walk through why DOUBLE_BAD(3 + 4) is wrong and how you would write DOUBLE_SAFE.
How do you safely write a multi-statement macro used in an if without braces?
What do # and ## do in a macro definition?

hints.1: Expand the macro on paper before thinking about runtime values.
hints.2: Precedence needs parentheses; side effects need single evaluation; multi-statement needs a statement wrapper.
hints.3: ((x)*2); double-eval if x appears twice; do { … } while (0); # → string, ## → glue tokens.

phases.goal: Decide when macros are justified versus const, enum, and inline, and when headers vs object files own definitions.

must_hit.point: Modern C prefers const/enum for values and inline functions for callable logic over macros because they give type safety, scope, and debugger visibility.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says prefer language features first; macros are a last resort.

must_hit.point: Use macros only when you must manipulate text: stringizing, token-pasting, __FILE__/__LINE__, do-while(0) control-flow shaping, conditional compilation, or type-agnostic ops like container_of that cannot be ordinary functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists text-only capabilities as the legitimate macro niche.

must_hit.point: Headers must hold declarations (signatures, macros, structs, types); putting definitions in a header included by multiple .c files yields multiple-definition linker errors.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates declaration vs definition and names the link-time multiple definition failure.

probes: When should you use a macro versus inline, const, or enum?
What belongs in a header file versus a .c file regarding definitions?

hints.1: Ask what macros cannot express that the language can.
hints.2: Type safety and single evaluation favor inline/const/enum; text ops favor macros.
hints.3: const/enum/inline by default; macros for #, ##, __FILE__, conditional compilation, container_of; headers = declarations only.

phases.goal: Apply preprocessor idioms used in real systems code and debugging builds.

must_hit.point: ARRAY_SIZE(arr) is (sizeof(arr) / sizeof((arr)[0])) for element count of a statically allocated array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes or states total bytes divided by bytes of the first element.

must_hit.point: container_of(ptr, type, member) recovers the containing struct pointer via (char*)ptr minus offsetof(type, member), enabling intrusive generic structures (Linux kernel staple).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains member pointer → enclosing struct via offsetof subtraction.

must_hit.point: assert from <assert.h> reports failure with __FILE__ and __LINE__; defining NDEBUG before including <assert.h> compiles asserts away. Predefined macros include __FILE__, __LINE__, __DATE__, __TIME__ (__func__ is a predefined identifier, not a macro).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties assert location printing to those macros and NDEBUG stripping asserts in release.

probes: Write or explain the ARRAY_SIZE macro.
What is container_of used for, and how does it work at a high level?
How does assert know file and line, and what does NDEBUG change?

hints.1: Think sizeof of the whole array versus one element.
hints.2: ARRAY_SIZE divides sizes; container_of subtracts member offset; assert uses predefined location macros.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer const or enum for constants and inline functions for callable logic for type safety, scope, and debugger visibility. Reserve macros for text-only needs: #, ##, __FILE__/__LINE__, do-while(0) statement shaping, conditional compilation, and type-agnostic idioms like container_of.
Use <> for system/standard and third-party headers (system search paths). Use "" for project headers (current source directory first, then system fallback).

Both prevent double inclusion per translation unit. Traditional #ifndef/#define/#endif is portable standard practice; #pragma once is a widely supported extension that avoids naming collisions and can compile slightly faster.

tradeoffs.topic: Declarations in headers vs definitions in headers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Headers should contain declarations only. Definitions of functions or variables in headers included by multiple .c files produce multiple-definition linker errors.

gotchas.trap: Function-like macro without parentheses around parameters and the whole body (e.g. DOUBLE_BAD / SQUARE).
gotchas.correction: Wrap every parameter use and the entire replacement list so expansion preserves intended precedence (e.g. ((x) * 2) or ((x) * (x))).

gotchas.trap: Passing side-effecting arguments to a macro that uses a parameter more than once (double-eval), even with safe parentheses—e.g. SQUARE_SAFE(i++) → ((i++) * (i++)).
gotchas.correction: There is no standard C macro fix; use an inline function so the argument is evaluated once. Multiple modification without a sequence point is undefined behavior.

gotchas.trap: Multi-statement macro used in brace-less if/else so only the first statement is conditional and the rest always run.
gotchas.correction: Wrap the body in do { … } while (0) so it is one statement, executes once, and requires a trailing semicolon.

gotchas.trap: Putting function or variable definitions in a header included by multiple translation units.
gotchas.correction: Keep only declarations in headers; put definitions in a single .c file to avoid link-time multiple definition errors.

gotchas.trap: Assuming __func__ is a predefined macro like __FILE__ / __LINE__.
gotchas.correction: __func__ is a predefined identifier providing the function name, not a macro.
